item.description: Welcome to the online digital collection of the Maine State Archives, a bureau within the Department of the Secretary of State. We maintain approximately 8 miles of official state records (both paper and digital) that are deemed permanently valuable. These records include bills introduced in the Legislature, reports from the Governor's Executive Council, election returns, deeds and maps from the Maine Land Office, vital statistics prior to 1892, federal census records up to 1880, county court records dating back to 1636, and military records through World War I, among others. As of March 1, 2026, our online collection includes over one million individual records. The Maine State Archives will continue to expand this database as we digitize more of our collection. All documents are public records and are free to download. item.description: First printing since 1876 includes redacted indigenous treaty obligations AUGUSTA, MAINE – Secretary of State Shenna Bellows marked Constitution Day by formally unveiling the official printing of the Maine Constitution, the first formal printing since 1876. The unveiling took place at the Maine State Cultural Center in Augusta and included displays of the original 1820 copy of the Maine State Constitution and the 1876 version along with the new printing. For more than a century, Maine omitted three original sections – Sections 1, 2 and 5, of Article X of the Constitution – from official printed copies. The sections, which remained in full force despite the redaction, include treaty obligations to the Wabanaki tribal nations. In 2023, Mainers voted overwhelmingly to cancel the 1876 amendment compelling the redaction and restore the language to printed copies of the constitution. “Restoring this language to the Maine Constitution is a visible and lasting reminder of the important role the Wabanaki people played in the formation of Maine,” said Secretary Bellows. “The Wabanaki have existed in Maine for 13,000 years, and voters made it clear that their immeasurable contributions to our collective past, present and future should be known, acknowledged and celebrated, not hidden from history.” The large format version was printed using a 19th century letterpress onto vellum by Wolfe Editions of Portland and will be permanently housed at the Maine State Archives along with the previous versions. ###

First printing since 1876 includes redacted indigenous treaty obligations

AUGUSTA, MAINE – Secretary of State Shenna Bellows marked Constitution Day by formally unveiling the official printing of the Maine Constitution, the first formal printing since 1876. The unveiling took place at the Maine State Cultural Center in Augusta and included displays of the original 1820 copy of the Maine State Constitution and the 1876 version along with the new printing.

For more than a century, Maine omitted three original sections – Sections 1, 2 and 5, of Article X of the Constitution – from official printed copies. The sections, which remained in full force despite the redaction, include treaty obligations to the Wabanaki tribal nations. In 2023, Mainers voted overwhelmingly to cancel the 1876 amendment compelling the redaction and restore the language to printed copies of the constitution. 

“Restoring this language to the Maine Constitution is a visible and lasting reminder of the important role the Wabanaki people played in the formation of Maine,” said Secretary Bellows. “The Wabanaki have existed in Maine for 13,000 years, and voters made it clear that their immeasurable contributions to our collective past, present and future should be known, acknowledged and celebrated, not hidden from history.”

The large format version was printed using a 19th century letterpress onto vellum by Wolfe Editions of Portland and will be permanently housed at the Maine State Archives along with the previous versions.

This rule prohibits federal matching funds for puberty blockers, cross-sex hormone therapy, and surgical interventions when used for gender transition for Medicaid beneficiaries under 18 and CHIP enrollees under 19. The rule does not prohibit states from using state-only funds to cover these services. Maine law requires MaineCare to cover medically necessary treatment for or related to gender dysphoria and protects members from discrimination based on gender identity or gender expression. Providers should continue to provide these services as usual. Specific guidance for providers on Maine’s implementation of state-only coverage, including billing guidance, will be forthcoming. To help ensure MaineCare members receive the health care services they need, and have the information necessary to make informed decisions, OMS will continue to communicate with members about covered services through the Member Handbook and the OMS website . Clarification of Funding for Gender-Affirming Care

Sep 18, 2026

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) published a final rule in the Federal Register on August 13, 2026, that limits federal Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) funding for certain gender-affirming medical care provided to minors, scheduled to take effect October 13, 2026. This rule prohibits federal matching funds for puberty blockers, cross-sex hormone therapy, and surgical interventions when used for gender transition for Medicaid beneficiaries under 18 and CHIP enrollees under 19.  

The rule does not prohibit states from using state-only funds to cover these services. Maine law requires MaineCare to cover medically necessary treatment for or related to gender dysphoria and protects members from discrimination based on gender identity or gender expression.  

Providers should continue to provide these services as usual. Specific guidance for providers on Maine’s implementation of state-only coverage, including billing guidance, will be forthcoming.  

To help ensure MaineCare members receive the health care services they need, and have the information necessary to make informed decisions, OMS will continue to communicate with members about covered services through the Member Handbook and the OMS website.  

For questions, please contact Provider Relations Specialist, Lisa Bouchard.

Chapter 302: SALES TO GOVERNMENTAL AGENCIES AND EXEMPT ORGANIZATIONS
SUMMARY: Establishes administrative rules regarding tax-exempt sales and explains the circumstances under which a retailer or service provider will be relieved of its burden of proving that sales to an entity described in 36 M.R.S. §§ 1760 or 2557, including an agency or instrumentality of the federal government or of the State of Maine, are exempt from Maine sales, or use, or service provider tax.
SECTION 1. Exempt sales generally; burden of proof 1. Generally Sales and Use Tax. Sales to certain organizations and governmental agencies are exempt from sales and use tax pursuant to 36 M.R.S. § 1760. Pursuant to 36 M.R.S. § 1760-C, an exemption provided by 36 M.R.S. § 1760 to a person based upon its charitable, nonprofit , or other public purposes applies only if the property or service purchased is intended to be used by the person primarily in the activity identified by the particular exemption. The burden of proving a sale is to an organization that is exempt under 36 M.R.S. § 1760 is on the person making the sale. The retailer is relieved of this burden of proof if it satisfies the provisions of this rule. 2. Certain purchases subject to tax. The Employment Situation in Maine - August 2026

September 18, 2026

Released: 10 a.m. Friday, September 18, 2026

Contact: Mark McInerney, (207) 620-0197

The 3.2 unemployment rate in August changed little from July. Nonfarm wage and salary jobs have remained within a narrow range for 28 consecutive months.

Seasonally Adjusted Statewide Labor Force Estimates

The 3.2 percent unemployment rate changed little from recent months. Unemployment rates have remained within a narrow range between 3.1 and 3.3 percent for 24 consecutive months. Unemployment has been below 4 percent for 56 months, the longest duration on record. Maine's unemployment rate has been below the U.S. average for more than 18 years, and remains below the long-term average of 5.4 percent for the state since 1976. Unemployment averaged 4.1 percent for New England and 4.1 percent for the U.S. in the month.

The labor force participation rate averaged 58.8 percent over the last three months, lower than during the three months through May. A decreasing employment-to-population ratio in the three months through August is the primary reason for lower rates of labor force participation.

Seasonally Adjusted Statewide Nonfarm Jobs Estimates

Preliminary seasonally adjusted estimates indicate that in August, nonfarm wage and salary jobs were little changed from July. Employment levels were stable in every sector.

Job estimates have stayed within a narrow range near 660,000 for 28 consecutive months (estimates ranging less than 0.5 percent higher or lower each month). Over the last year, job increases in the health care and social assistance, and retail trade sectors were offset by modest decreases across several sectors.

Not Seasonally Adjusted County and Metro Area Labor Force Estimates

On a not seasonally adjusted basis, the statewide unemployment rate was 3.1 percent. Rates were at least 0.3 percentage points higher than that in seven counties, at least 0.3 points lower than that in four, and close to the average in five. Rates were lowest in the coastal counties and highest along the northern rim of the state.

Among the three metro areas, unemployment was below the statewide average in Portland-S. Portland, and close to the average in Bangor and Lewiston-Auburn.

Not Seasonally Adjusted Statewide and Metro Area Hours and Earnings Estimates

The private sector workweek averaged 33.5 hours and earnings averaged $33.77 per hour in August. Average hours changed little, and hourly earnings increased 4.2 percent from one year ago. The workweek was longest in the construction and manufacturing sectors and shortest in the leisure and hospitality sector. Earnings were highest in professional and business services and lowest in leisure and hospitality. Hourly earnings were above the statewide average in Portland-S. Portland and below it in the Bangor and Lewiston-Auburn metros.

Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

You know, when I took office nearly eight years ago, I promised that Maine won't wait to take action to protect our state, our people, and our economy from the dangers of extreme weather events caused by pollution and changes to our environment. And I promised that we would fight to preserve this special place that we call home; preserve it for the benefit of our children and grandchildren.

The stakes could not be higher. Look no further than the devastating storms of just a few years ago. Storms that impacted our communities, our people, and our economy—that destroyed a lot of infrastructure across the state.

I've made climate action a cornerstone of my Administration. First, we created the Maine Climate Council, and we issued a groundbreaking climate action plan. And we dedicated millions of federal and state dollars to make that plan a reality.

In 2025, we made the single largest investment in storm recovery by any administration in Maine history, and we created the State Resilience Office to build better, stronger public infrastructure to withstand future storms.

That office manages a partnership of more than 300 communities and has awarded more than $29 million in state and federal funds for projects to prepare local communities for flooding, for storm surge, for rising sea levels, and other climate and weather events that put people's lives and livelihoods at risk.

Recently, I was proud to announce the latest round of funding through that partnership: more than $4.7 million in grants to 72 cities and Tribal Governments, including the towns of Bingham and Madawaska:

  • The Town of Bingham will install high-efficiency heat pumps and a rooftop solar system in order to lower their energy costs at the municipally owned Veterans Building;
  • The Town of Madawaska will use their grant to launch the RIDER Program, a shared e-bike fleet in a rural community that doesn't have public transportation;
  • And the Town of Freedom will use its grant to do an energy audit of its buildings and to plan for a bridge replacement across Hustus Brook.

Through these projects and so many more, we are continuing to address the very real threat of severe weather events for the health of our people, the health of our environment, and the health of our economy.

You know that clean air and clean water know no political party. Our planet is neither Democratic nor Republican. It's the home of all of us, and it is the responsibility of all of us and all governments to preserve it for future generations.

I am proud that over the past nearly eight years, we've made cost-effective heat pumps, weatherization programs, and other things available for Maine people and businesses. We've attracted investments in emerging industries and renewables, and we've created good-paying, green collar jobs. We've reduced our reliance on expensive fossil fuels, and we've mobilized scientists, industry leaders, local and state officials, and young people from all over to act as one to address the effects of climate change.

We won't wait for the next storm or the next disaster. We do care. And as the author Wendell Berry wrote, "We care for this home that is ours. A home that we care for as we care for no other place in the world."

This is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Maine's Minimum Wage to Increase to $15.70 Per Hour in 2027

September 18, 2026

For Immediate Release: September 18, 2026

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

AUGUSTA - The Maine Department of Labor announced today that, effective January 1, 2027, the state minimum wage will increase from $15.10 to $15.70 per hour, based on data recently made available by the U.S. Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics. MDOL is required under Maine law (Maine statute Title 26, chapter 7, section 664) to make annual adjustments to the minimum wage based on the cost-of-living index (CPI-W) for the Northeast Region, after Maine voters amended the law by referendum in 2016. Between August 2025 and August 2026, there was a 4.1 percent increase in the CPI-W.

According to the U.S. Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey for 2025, there were 28,000 hourly workers who were paid less than $15.00 per hour. These workers represent about four percent of all wage and salary workers (both paid at hourly rates and not paid at hourly rates) and about eight percent of wage and salary workers who are paid at hourly rates.

Agricultural workers in Maine are also entitled to the state minimum wage, after the Legislature enacted and Governor Mills signed "An Act to Establish a State Minimum Hourly Wage for Agricultural Workers" in 2025.

The "tip wage," or service employee minimum wage, will increase from $7.55 to $7.85 per hour. This means that service employees must receive a direct cash wage of at least $7.85 per hour from the employer. The employer must be able to show that the employee receives at least the minimum wage of $15.70 per hour when the direct wage and tips are combined at the end of the week. The amount of tips necessary to qualify as a service employee will increase from $191 to $199 per month.

The minimum salary threshold for exempting a worker from overtime pay must exceed 3,000 times the State's minimum wage or the annualized rate established by the U.S. Department of Labor, whichever is higher. Starting January 1, 2027, the new minimum salary threshold for salaried workers exempt from overtime will be $905.79 per week, or $47,101.08 per year. This is only one of the factors used in determining whether a worker is exempt from overtime pay under federal or state law. An individual can earn more than the minimum salary threshold and still be eligible for overtime. The duties of each worker must be considered as part of this analysis.

Employers can download the required minimum wage poster at no cost on the Department's website.

The minimum wage and overtime law can be found here.

Attention Trading Partners: MIHMS Upgrade October Payment Cycle Changes and System Access Limitations

Sep 21, 2026

As previously communicated, the Office of MaineCare Services (OMS) is preparing to launch an upgraded version of MIHMS, MaineCare’s claims processing system. The upgrade is currently scheduled to go live on October 10, 2026. To support a smooth transition, OMS must implement temporary system access limitations and adjustments to payment cycles in October.  

From Friday, October 2 at 8:00 PM until Monday, October 12 at 8:00 AM, MIHMS will be in a “data freeze” while OMS completes final system readiness and transition activities. 

Please note that we have updated the FAQ previously shared, as of September 21, 2026. 

Changes to October payment cycles:   

Review this information and plan billing accordingly to prepare for the transition.

  *As always, timely submission does not guarantee that the claim will process in time for the next payment cycle. OMS may take up to 30 days to process and pay a claim, depending on any edits or issues that may cause the claim to pend for manual review, as well as other processing requirements that may require the full 30-day timeframe. 

Preparing for the changes to October payment cycles: 

The HealthPAS Online Portal has returned to its previous regular operating hours. Providers again have 24/7 access to the portal, for additional flexibility and time to submit claims outside of standard business hours.   

We strongly encourage providers to submit claims approaching timely filing limits in the next few weeks to avoid potential submission delays. The planned data freeze does not modify existing Medicaid timely filing requirements. Providers remain responsible for ensuring claims are submitted within the established timely filing guidelines. 

Other system access limitations: 

Providers can find other expected impacts of the data freeze in this FAQ. We have updated the FAQ as of September 21, 2026. Topics include: 

  • HealthPAS Online Portal, including impacts on submitting claims, submitting prior authorizations, and checking member eligibility 
  • Provider Enrollment Application (PEA) 
  • Value-Based Purchasing Management System (VMS) Portal 
  • Paper & fax document submissions 
  • Provider Services & Member Services call centers 
  • Value Added Network (VAN) Trading Partners 
  • Prior authorizations for prescriptions and behavioral health services 
  • Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) 
  • Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) 

You can also check the OMS Provider Resources webpage, in the first box of information called “Health PAS Online Portal,” for the most recent information about the upgrade.

Reminders in Preparation for Maine eCourts and eFiling in Cumberland County Courts

Date: 9/23/2026

On Monday, September 28, 2026, the Maine Judicial Branch is expanding Maine eCourts to all case types in Judicial Region 2, comprising Cumberland County Unified Criminal Docket (UCD), Cumberland County Superior Court, Portland District Court, and Bridgton District Court.

All case types -- civil, family, juvenile and criminal cases -- will be included in the transition from paper filing to electronic filing. As of Monday, September 28, all mandatory electronic filers pursuant to the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems (MRECS) will be required to eFile documents in these courts. Self-represented litigants (parties who do not have attorneys) who file fewer than six cases in a calendar year will not be required to eFile.

Court Closures and Emergency Filing Procedures
To prepare for the implementation of Maine eCourts and eFiling on September 28, Region 2 courts are currently operating on a modified schedule and have emergency filing procedures in place. In addition, all Region 2 courts will be closed from 8 a.m. to noon the week of September 28th. Please refer to the schedule of closures and emergency procedures during these closings.

ShareFile Discontinued in Region 2 Courts
The ShareFile platform used in Region 2 courts will be disabled for all criminal, civil violation, juvenile filings, and GAL vouchers, at 2:00 p.m. on Thursday, September 24. Starting Monday, September 28, attorneys must instead use eFileMaine. Please note, attorney vouchers filed pursuant to the Standing Order regarding Payment to Court-Appointed Counsel will continue to be accepted by ShareFile for a grace period of 60 days.

Training Resources
For attorneys and staff who are new to using eFileMaine, we highly recommend viewing the recorded videos, particularly the video excerpts, available on the Maine eCourts Trainings and Resources web page. In addition to the recordings, the information and resources available on the Maine eCourts Trainings and Resources web page offer guidance for setting up your eFileMaine account and instructions to eFile documents successfully.

Personal Identifying Information (PII) Attachment (CR-CV-JV-297)
Pursuant to the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems (MRECS) filers are responsible for omitting or redacting nonpublic information in electronically filed documents. If the filer decides to omit rather than redact, the personal identifying information must be included on this form.

The PII form should be uploaded as an attachment to the associated filing document, in the same way that an exhibit is submitted.

Online Fine Payments
As of September 28th, parties who wish to make criminal fine payments online for cases in Cumberland County will be directed to the new online payment portal, Maine eCourts Criminal Fines and Fees. Visit Maine eCourts: Pay a Court Fine to learn more.

Support
Support for eFiling is available by emailing ecourtshelp@courts.maine.gov or by calling (207) 213-2813, Monday through Thursday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

For more information on Maine eCourts and eFiling, visit: https://www.courts.maine.gov/ecourts/index.html

item.title: US Department of Labor cites New Jersey car wash for willfully exposing workers to safety hazards, proposes more than $446K in fines — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
item.description: SICKLERVILLE, NJ – The U.S. Department of Labor has cited a New Jersey car wash service for willfully exposing workers to safety hazards related to hazardous energy and excessive noise levels, proposing $446,864 in penalties.The department’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration found that ModWash LLC, an express car wash service operating multiple locations throughout the country, including five in Sicklerville, willfully exposed workers to hazardous energy by failing to lock out equipment prior to conducting maintenance activities and not using energy control procedures. The agency also cited ModWash for two repeat violations for failing to have clear lockout procedures and specific instructions for controlling all energy sources and not training employees on equipment lockout/tagout processes. In addition, the employer was cited for five serious violations for failing to develop and implement a noise monitoring program, establish a baseline audiogram for employees within six months of exposure, train employees exposed to noise above 85 decibels, provide lockout/tagout devices, and attach such devices to machines prior to servicing them.The company has 15 business days from receipt of their citations and penalties to comply, request an informal conference with OSHA, or contest the findings before the independent Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission. Check the OSHA establishment search page periodically for any changes in the inspection or penalty status.Visit OSHA’s website for information on developing a workplace safety and health program. Employers can also contact the agency for information about OSHA’s compliance assistance resources and for free help on complying with OSHA standards.

As a reminder, all providers who deliver services following the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) must ensure all MaineCare-covered services are documented following the Department of Health and Human Services/Maine Department of Education Joint IEP Guidance document. 

The Maine Department of Education has released updated Joint IEP Guidance to help schools follow federal and state requirements. The updated guidance was developed through a collaborative effort and is available on the MaineCare in Education web page. 

DOE first released the Joint Guidance on August 28, 2026, and has re-issued this guidance effective September 18, 2026. The reissued guidance replaces the previously issued Joint Guidance and provides clarification in response to questions and feedback received from School Administrative Units (SAUs), providers, and other interested parties. 

All IEP documents must reflect the updated guidance as soon as possible, but no later than thirty (30) days of the issuance of the guidance.

For technical assistance regarding the billing and processing of MaineCare claims, please contact your Provider Relations Specialist.

For technical information related to IEP development, please contact Dan Hemdal at the Maine Department of Education.

OSHA’s new guidance, “Opioid Overdose Rescue with Reversal Medications,” is part of the Great American Recovery Initiative, a government-wide effort by the Trump Administration prioritizing addiction treatment and recovery. The fact sheet provides practical information that focuses on empowering workplaces to recognize the signs of an overdose and act immediately.“President Trump has charged the Department of Labor with making recovery part of our workforce strategy, helping more individuals return to work and ensuring our businesses have the workers they need,” said Acting Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “Today’s guidance, released as part of President Trump’s Great American Recovery Initiative, is exactly the kind of action we were tasked with delivering on for the American people.”“President Trump has been fighting back against the deadly synthetic opioids infecting the entire illicit drug supply, from known illicit drugs to counterfeit tablets sold on the street or through fake online pharmacies,” said White House Drug Czar Sara Carter. “Because fentanyl has infiltrated the illicit drug landscape and acts as a chemical weapon against our people, it is critically important that the American workforce is familiar with drug overdose recognition and reversal. I am grateful to the Department of Labor for informing employers and workers about life-saving overdose reversal treatments like naloxone.”OSHA’s fact sheet highlights key opioid overdose preparedness strategies, including:Keep lifesaving FDA-approved reversal medications – such as naloxone or nalmefene – on hand. These safe, life-saving medications quickly restore normal breathing and generally have no effect if opioids are not present.Treat overdose kits like first aid by storing them in highly visible, easily accessible locations, just like automated external defibrillators or standard first-aid kits.Educate workers on how to identify critical symptoms of an overdose, such as slow or stopped breathing, blue lips or skin, pinpoint pupils, or unresponsiveness.Prepare for rapid action in an emergency by training workers to administer the medication, safely position the individual, and provide supportive care while waiting for first responders.OSHA’s guidance emphasizes that while these medications are critical, they do not replace emergency services. Attorney General Frey, along with the Attorneys General of 47 other states and territories, announce preliminary approval of their plan to distribute funds to consumers following multiple settlements with drug manufacturers accused of conspiring to inflate prices of generic drugs.

AUGUSTA – Attorney General Frey is urging consumers to check their eligibility for compensation for certain generic drug purchases and to submit a claim for compensation. This month, the U.S. District Court for the District of Connecticut granted preliminary approval of a plan, filed by Maine and a coalition of 47 other states and territories, to distribute settlement funds paid by generic drug manufacturers in exchange for settlement of claims that those companies illegally conspired to raise the prices of generic drugs.

The coalition previously announced settlements with the manufacturers Glenmark, Lannett, Bausch, Apotex, Heritage, and Heritage’s parent company, Emcure, totaling approximately $96.5 million. The multistate coalition’s distribution plan aims to return millions of dollars from those settlement funds to those potentially harmed by the elevated prices of the generic drugs that are the subjects of those settlements.

If you purchased a listed generic drug between May 2009 and December 2019, you may be eligible for compensation. To determine your eligibility, call 1-866-290-0182 (Toll-Free), email info@AGGenericDrugs.com or visit https://www.AGGenericDrugs.com. The deadline for submitting a claim is March 8, 2027.

Maine is part of a coalition of nearly all states and territories engaged in a series of antitrust cases, starting first in 2016. The first complaint included Heritage and 17 other corporate defendants, two individual defendants, and 15 generic drugs. The second complaint was filed in 2019 against Teva Pharmaceuticals and 21 of the nation’s largest generic drug manufacturers. The complaint names 16 individual senior executive defendants. The third complaint, to be tried first, focuses on 80 topical generic drugs that account for billions of dollars of sales in the United States and names 26 corporate defendants and 10 individual defendants. The States filed a fourth complaint earlier this year, alleging that Novartis AG, Sandoz Group AG and Sandoz AG, are liable for Sandoz’s alleged conduct and for fraudulently transferring assets. Seven pharmaceutical executives have been cooperating to support the States’ claims in these cases.

Maine Department of Labor announces October workplace safety and labor law training schedule

September 24, 2026

For Immediate Release: Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

AUGUSTA - The Maine Department of Labor offers free workplace safety and labor law training to help employers, managers, supervisors, human resources professionals and others understand workplace safety requirements and Maine labor laws. The Department has announced its schedule of October classes, with trainings offered through SafetyWorks! and the Bureau of Labor Standards.

Registration is required, and space may be limited. View the October schedule and register for a class.

Unless otherwise noted, classes are held at the SafetyWorks! Training Institute at the Maine Department of Labor, 45 Commerce Drive in Augusta.

October Class Schedule

Fire Extinguisher/Emergency Action Plans/Workplace Violence Thursday, Oct. 1, 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.
SafetyWorks! Training Institute, Augusta

Workplace emergencies include fire, medical, and workplace violence. This course covers the requirements of an emergency action plan, fire extinguisher use, and considering the potential for workplace violence. The SWTI Lab includes a fire extinguisher discharge activity to assist participants in learning how to use a fire extinguisher.

Bloodborne Pathogens Train-the-Trainer Friday, Oct. 2, 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. SafetyWorks! Training Institute, Augusta

This half-day class provides guidance on what is needed to be compliant with the bloodborne pathogen standard. This course will review written program requirements, training, documentation, Hepatitis B, and sharp logs.

Safety & Health Management Systems Tuesday, Oct. 6, 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. SafetyWorks! Training Institute, Augusta

Successful safety and health programs are more than just compliance with the OSHA standards. Injuries and illnesses are reduced when employers possess common elements to identify and address safety and health hazards. This course outlines roles and responsibilities, common principles, required functions and programs of a successful safety and health management system. This course prepares organizations who would like to pursue SHARP/ SHAPE.

SafetyWorks! Training Institute, Augusta

Whether your employees work outside or inside, cold and hot temperatures can be hazardous to their health. This class covers cold and heat temperature illnesses, signs and symptoms, and control measures to prevent and treat temperature related injuries.

SafetyWorks! Training Institute, Augusta

This class covers the requirements of the welding standard, in addition to the storage and proper use of compressed gas. Proper inspection techniques of hoses, torches, and regulators will be demonstrated.

As fall arrives in Maine, respiratory viruses such as influenza (flu), COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), also return and begin to spread more widely as people spend more time together, indoors. The Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) reminds Maine people and visitors to take steps to keep themselves, their loved ones, and neighbors healthy this respiratory virus season.

Respiratory viruses can cause fever, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle aches, and fatigue. Some people are more likely to get very sick and need medical attention. These viruses can spread when an infected person coughs or sneezes. They can also spread from touching the surface with the virus on it and then touching your nose or mouth before washing your hands.

The Maine CDC recommends the following measures to protect yourself and others:

  • Stay home when you are sick.
  • Wash your hands frequently with soap and water.
  • Clean and disinfect surfaces and objects that people touch often.
  • If you are sick, consider wearing a mask around others.
  • Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or your elbow.
  • Avoid close contact with people who are sick.
  • Get vaccinated, as appropriate for flu, COVID-19, and RSV.

Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent respiratory viruses. Vaccines can also help make illness less severe and help prevent missed work or school. Getting a flu vaccine every year and staying up to date with COVID-19 and RSV vaccinations, if eligible, can help lower the risk of getting sick.

Consistent with the recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the Maine CDC recommends the following respiratory virus immunization for the 2026-2027 season:

  • Flu: Everyone 6 months and older should receive an annual flu vaccine.
  • COVID-19: Vaccination is recommended for
    • all children ages 6 through 23 months;
    • children and adolescents ages 2 through 18 years who are at increased risk for severe COVID-19 or who want to be vaccinated;
    • adults age 19 and older;
    • pregnant individuals.
  • RSV: Immunization is recommended for certain infants, pregnant people, and older adults.
    • Infants: RSV immunization is recommended for those younger than 8 months born during or entering their first RSV season, if they are not protected by maternal RSV vaccination.
      • Certain children ages 8-19 months who are at increased risk for severe RSV may also be recommended to receive RSV immunization during their second season.
    • Pregnant people: RSV vaccination is recommended during weeks 32 through 36 of pregnancy.
    • Older adults: All adults age 75 and older and adults 50-74 at increased risk for severe RSV illness.

To find the nearest location to get a vaccine, contact your local pharmacy or health care provider.

(Yokohama), located in the state of Coahuila, Mexico, are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. This follows the recent closure of the Yokohama tire manufacturing plant in Salem, Virginia and the layoff of nearly 600 American workers. The United States will suspend the liquidation of all entries of goods into this country from the Yokohama facility, which produces tires, until further notice.Today’s action demonstrates the Trump administration’s America First approach, which ensures our trade partners do not undermine worker protections to gain an unfair trade advantage or attract investment. The Secretary of Labor and United States Trade Representative co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On August 26, 2026, the ILC received an RRM petition from the Liga Sindical Obrera Mexicana (LSOM), a Mexican labor union, and the International Lawyers Assisting Workers Network (ILAW). The petition alleges that Yokohama is violating workers’ rights to freedom of association and collective bargaining by retaliating against workers for engaging in union activity. These actions include engaging in unequal treatment against LSOM supporters, the denial of access to the plant for LSOM special delegates while granting unrestricted access to the representatives of a competing union, irregularities leading up to a Certificate of Representation vote, unlawful dismissals, and non-compliance with the sectoral collective bargaining agreement for the rubber manufacturing industry (known as the “contrato ley”). The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days. After conducting this review, the ILC determined that there is sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms. As a result, the United States Trade Representative has submitted a request to Mexico that Mexico review whether workers at Yokohama are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. Mexico has 10 days to agree to conduct a review and, if it agrees, 45 days from today to complete the review. The RRM, developed under the first Trump administration, is an unprecedented trade tool that works to level the playing field for American workers and businesses by addressing weak labor law enforcement in Mexican workplaces that compete in trade with the U.S. Read the request for review.Read the letter to the Secretary of the Treasury.View information about previous requests.Learn more about the department’s work to make global competition fair for American workers.

Voters urged to look for .gov websites for official, trusted voter information 

AUGUSTA, MAINE – Secretary of State Shenna Bellows today warned Mainers to be vigilant when viewing voting information online. This included raising awareness of private sites that may give the false impression – by name, URL, and/or design – that it is an official election website. 

“It is becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish what is real and what isn’t online,” said Secretary Bellows. “AI and other automated tools help partisan operatives or cybercriminals create websites that look official even when they’re not. While some non-governmental sites about voting present accurate information, many do not.”

Many sites are designed to encourage citizens to register to vote and may in fact redirect visitors to official sites. However, many sites may require visitors to enter their personal information before they are redirected. Official state addresses will include .gov. For example, Mainers can register to vote at https://www.maine.gov/vote or find official election information by visiting the Secretary of State’s website at https://www.maine.gov/sos. 

“If you don’t see .gov in the web address, it is not an official state government website,” Secretary Bellows said. “If you are being asked to enter personal information like name and email address before you get to an official .gov link, then someone else is getting your private data. Instead of giving out private information to sites that might try to scam you or steal your data, go straight to the source at maine.gov/vote.”  

Secretary Bellows also encouraged voters to be careful when viewing election information on social media and always research and vet the information that they read. 

“There is unfortunately so much misinformation and disinformation out there, it can be overwhelming and difficult to know what’s true and what’s not,” said Secretary Bellows. “Everyone can play a part in reducing anxiety about the upcoming election by going to official sources and not sharing or posting unvetted and potentially false content. We have had safe, free, and secure elections in Maine for over 200 years, and we expect the same this November.”

Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Well, last week I was privileged to witness a group of multinational soldiers complete a joint military exercise known as the Common Challenge 2026. Up in the mountains of Montenegro, among the chatter of many nations, I listened to dignitaries and servicemembers comment on the success of the day, on the readiness for the mission, and on the grit and pride of that international team.

My thoughts turned to Shakespeare, a bard of some four centuries ago, who could not have envisioned the future circumstances which we find ourselves in today, but who said prophetically and for all time: "the Readiness is all."

Readiness indeed. Readiness is what I saw in Montenegro last week. Readiness for things known and unknown, unexpected and expected.

I traveled there with Major General Diane Dunn and Maine National Guardsmen to Montenegro to observe that joint training mission and to meet with Montenegrin officials, military members, and citizens to celebrate the 20th anniversary of Maine's strategic partnership with Montenegro. I am the second governor to have visited Montenegro and celebrate this partnership.

In 2006, Maine and Montenegro formed that partnership to share training and military expertise, as Montenegro became a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or NATO. Both the state of Maine and the people of Montenegro have benefited through this shared knowledge, through team exercises, and through progress in this strategic partnership.

Over the past 20 years, our servicemembers and Montenegrins have trained side-by-side, shoulder-to-shoulder, learning how to navigate challenging mountain terrain, practicing difficult search and rescue missions, confronting dangerously cold weather conditions, and defending the security of our respective regions. Montenegrin soldiers have traveled to Maine for engineering projects, and Maine National Guardsmen have traveled to Montenegro to respond to cyber-attacks on that country. 

While in Montenegro, Major General Dunn and I met with the Prime Minister and the President, Defense Minister, and Foreign Minister of the country to discuss the future of our relationship and the prospects for more collaboration. Collaboration in forestry research, in deep port uses, in trade, and in educational exchanges for the benefit of both regions.

Maine, like Montenegro, for instance, has a deep ocean port, which is an important gateway for trade. We are tackling threats of cybersecurity and threats from severe weather caused by climate change, just as they are. We too have a thriving forest products industry that is at the heart of our economy.

So I emphasized to the Montenegrins that Maine offers world-leading universities, community colleges, and private higher eds, who are all ready to work with Montenegro students to train the next generation of best and brightest leaders—broadening research and bolstering our mutual security.

I am proud of our own Guard members and of their determination to reach outside their own boundaries and zones of operation and zones of comfort to assist the people of Montenegro in addressing cybersecurity threats, in training and in military preparedness, and in maximizing the potential for international collaboration and expertise.

To properly commemorate the 20th anniversary of this bilateral commitment of the Maine National Guard and the Armed Forces of Montenegro, I've officially proclaimed September 17th as Montenegro-Maine Partnership Day, reaffirming our friendship with the leaders, the people, and the Armed Forces of Montenegro.

Maine and Montenegro have contributed our human and physical resources to this effort, and our culture, our character, and our courage have combined for the common good of humanity and for the common peace of our nations.

Maine and Montenegro are ready.

This is Governor Janet Mills, and I thank you for listening.
